theme: India's jobless growth · 일자리 없는 성장

tracks.title: Is aircon the answer to a heating world?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Hi Neil.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Hi Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, Neil, we've just had a really hot summer in the UK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Did you have air conditioning in your house?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I didn't have air conditioning in my house.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I wish I had, because it was really hot and I couldn't sleep.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: No, I had one of those big fans, which didn't always do its job.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: But there is a really serious side to this.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Heat records continue to be broken around the world.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: You may be feeling that summers are getting too hot.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Have you been using air conditioning more to cope?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If so, you're not alone.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Experts are predicting that ten new air conditioning units will be installed every second for the next 30 years.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Today on 6 Minute English, we're talking about this and whether air conditioning really is the best way to cope with a warming world.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: As always, Neil, we'll start with a quiz question.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, modern air conditioning was invented in 1902, but what was it originally used for?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Is it: a) to protect people in hospitals, b) to dry ink, or c) to clean air?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, I have absolutely no idea, Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I'm going to guess and say c) clean air.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK, Neil, we'll find out the answer at the end of the programme.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Georgie, we've been talking about how uncomfortable the hot weather can make you feel in the summer.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Is air conditioning all about comfort, though?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: No, it's not just about comfort.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Summer heat can be a real health issue as well.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: It's thought that across Europe, over 30,000 people died as a result of this summer's heat.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Dr Radhika Khosla, an expert in climatology, told BBC World Service's The Climate Question how important air conditioning can be:

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: Actually, air conditioning is life-saving.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: You know, in Singapore, when Lee Kuan Yew was asked what made civilisation possible in the tropics, he said it was air conditioning.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: And there are so many large parts of the world where we would not be able to inhabit if we did not have air conditioning.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: So, Radhika is saying that air conditioning is life-saving.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It literally stops people from dying.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes, and she makes the point that there are many parts of the world that we would not be able to inhabit – that means live in – without this technology.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: So, it sounds like air conditioning has a lot of good things about it.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Is it all positive, though?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: There are some serious downsides.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, one big problem with air conditioning is the amount of energy it uses.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Let's hear more from Radhika talking to The Climate Question:

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: When air conditioning becomes the first, go-to solution for how we deal with the increased, prolonged and extreme heat that we're going to face and are facing, it places stresses across the system that are not able to be met.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: So, you know, we're going to see the grid collapse.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: We're going to see emissions rise.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: We're going to see all kinds of other impacts that actually are quite detrimental.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: And we reach a vicious cycle, because then you're in a world where it's getting warmer.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: We're using air conditioning to be able to protect ourselves.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: That's leading to more emissions and more energy use.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: That is then making the world warmer.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: And then we need more air conditioning.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: We heard about the grid.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: The grid is the network that distributes electricity across towns, cities and countries.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: If people are trying to use more electricity than it can cope with, then the grid can collapse – you get power cuts, which is when you can't get any electricity.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: We heard that air conditioning creates emissions, which can lead the world to warm up, which means we then need more air conditioning.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: This makes the world even warmer and so on.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And Radhika calls this a vicious cycle.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: A vicious cycle, or a vicious circle, is where a solution to a problem actually makes it worse, which means you have to do more and that makes the problem even worse still.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, that sounds like a bit of a problem.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: What are the solutions?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, Radhika says that there are some things we should try first before using air conditioning, which will still be important.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Here she is again talking to The Climate Question.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: So, one of the most important things is to do passive cooling first.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: Now, passive cooling is when we take steps to provide thermal comfort that are not energy intensive.

transcript.speaker: Dr Radhika Khosla
transcript.text: Some of the most important ones are first to cut solar gain, which is through things like shading.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Passive cooling is where you cool your house down without using a lot of energy.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes, heat from the sun can be blocked by shading, which could be with trees, curtains or blinds.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: So, passive cooling and shading – that sounds really easy.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Is it that simple?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: No, that's not all we have to do.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Radhika also talks about the importance of using sustainable energy to power the air conditioning that we still will need.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It's time, I think, for you to give the answer to the question you asked us.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes, Neil.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I asked you what modern air conditioning was used for when it was first invented in 1902.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: And I had a wild guess.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I said c) to clean air.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: But you know what?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I'm feeling pretty confident now.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Sadly, you are incorrect.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The correct answer was b) to dry ink.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: It was invented by Willis Carrier at a printing company in Brooklyn, New York.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with life-saving, which describes something that stops people from dying.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If it's possible to inhabit somewhere, that means it's possible to live there.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: The grid is the system or network that distributes electricity across towns, cities, and countries.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: A vicious cycle is where a solution to a problem also makes it worse, meaning the problem just keeps getting even worse as you try to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Passive cooling is where you make a building cooler without using a lot of power.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And shading is blocking the sun's light and heat.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Thank you for joining us.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Goodbye!

listening.task: 6 Minute English를 끝까지 듣고 아래 퀴즈에 답해 보세요. 시간이 남으면 The Daily로 이어가요.

quiz.q: Modern air conditioning was invented in 1902. What was it originally used for? a) to protect people in hospitals, b) to dry ink, c) to clean air
quiz.answer: b) to dry ink. 뉴욕 브루클린의 인쇄 회사에서 Willis Carrier가 발명했어요.

sentences.text: Heat records continue to be broken around the world.
sentences.ko: 전 세계에서 폭염 기록이 계속 깨지고 있어요.

sentences.text: No, it's not just about comfort. Summer heat can be a real health issue as well.
sentences.ko: 아니요, 편안함만의 문제가 아니에요. 여름 더위는 실제 건강 문제가 될 수도 있어요.

sentences.text: That's leading to more emissions and more energy use.
sentences.ko: 그게 배출과 에너지 사용을 더 늘리고 있어요.

sentences.text: So, it sounds like air conditioning has a lot of good things about it.
sentences.ko: 그러니까 에어컨에는 좋은 점이 많은 것 같네요.

reading.title: What to make of 25 years of Narendra Modi
reading.summaryKo: 인도는 모디 정부 25년 동안 매년 약 7%씩 성장했지만 제조업과 사무직 일자리는 거의 늘지 않았어요. 그래서 젊은 층의 불만이 커지고 있다는 글이에요.
excerpt: No two lives move in perfect parallel. But the careers of Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping, both born in the early 1950s, have a certain symmetry. A quarter of a century ago each was running one of his country's coastal, industrial provinces. Mr Xi said he devoted the "prime" of his life to governing Fujian, in China's south-east. Meanwhile Mr Modi had just become chief minister of Gujarat, in India's west. Each used regional success as a springboard to the top.
And yet, that is not enough. A lesson from Mr Xi's China is that countries must work fast to grow rich before they get old. Unfortunately, the structure of India's economy is changing too slowly.
reading.tip: "And yet, that is not enough." 앞에서 칭찬을 늘어놓은 뒤 반전할 때 쓰는 Economist 특유의 표현이에요. 대화에서도 그대로 쓸 수 있어요.

vocab.example: Fast growth alone will not placate millions of young people looking for work.
He used his record in Gujarat as a springboard to national power.
Young graduates clamour for secure office jobs.
The anger is unlikely to abate without more good jobs.

vocab.meaning: (조금) 움직이다, 변하다 · barely budged = 거의 그대로
vocab.example: The share of farm workers has barely budged in 25 years.
India never went through the structural change that lifted East Asia.
Critics describe India's boom as jobless growth.

writing.prompt: What is the article's main point? Write 1–3 sentences in English.
writing.question: Why does the article compare Gujarat with Fujian?
writing.hint: 25년 전 두 사람이 맡은 해안 공업 지역이에요. 1인당 소득 (약 5배 vs 10배 이상)과 농업 종사자 비율 (45%→42% vs 46%→13%)을 비교해 보세요.

speaking.prompt: In one minute, explain to a friend why India's fast growth is not making young people happy.
phrases: On the one hand, ... On the other hand, ...
speaking.alt: 쉬운 버전: Do you use air conditioning at home? What else do you do to stay cool in summer?

evening.note: 첫날이라 1~10페이지예요. 모르는 단어는 3개까지만 표시하고 그냥 읽어 나가요.
